tip: To report what someone would do, the verb becomes a noun: 'edeceğini' means 'that he would do', and 'bildirdi' (informed) reports it.
The -ar ending normally states timeless facts: 'doğar' (rises) and 'batar' (sets) tell what the sun always does.
'keşke' means if only and pairs with a verb in -se: 'keşke ... gidebilsek' means I wish we could go.
The -meden ending means without doing: 'çay içmeden' means without drinking tea.
Adding -ince to a verb means when or as soon as: 'yaz gelince' means when summer comes.
-ebilir added to a verb means can or could: 'gez' plus -ebilir gives 'gezebilir', so 'gezebilir miyiz' asks could we wander.
The -ip ending links two verbs done by one person: 'giyinip evden çıktım' means got dressed and left the house, only the last verb fully conjugated.
The -mış ending marks something heard or inferred, not witnessed: 'varmış' means there apparently was, and 'yapılmış', apparently built.
Proper names take an apostrophe before case endings: 'Ankara'da' means in Ankara, the -da part meaning in or at.
To ask someone for something, put -dan on the person: 'komşudan ... istedim' is literally requested from the neighbor.
'hiçbir şey' (nothing) still needs a negative verb: 'hiçbir şey istemedim', both halves negative, means wanted nothing.
Adding -la to a noun tells how an action happens: 'şaşkınlıkla' means with surprise, from 'şaşkınlık' plus -la.
'yardım etmek' (to help) takes the -e ending, since help goes to someone: hence 'birbirlerine', to each other, carries -e.
'beri' (since) follows a noun ending in -tan/-den: 'sabahtan beri' means since morning, 'sabah' plus -tan plus 'beri'.
Possession marks both words: in 'annemin yemekleri' the owner takes -in and the thing owned takes -leri.
After a length of time, 'önce' means ago: 'üç yıl önce' is three years ago.
The -mış past reports something not personally witnessed: 'gelmiş' means it has come, so the story goes, unlike plain 'geldi'.
Comparison uses -dan plus 'daha': 'yaz aylarından çok daha soğuk' means much colder than summer months.
The -ir/-ar ending marks habits: 'gelir' and 'yapar' mean she regularly comes and cooks, not a one-time event.
Clock times take the -de/-te ending: 'saat üçte' means at three o'clock.
'sonra' (after) follows a noun ending in -ten/-tan: 'yemekten sonra' means after the meal, 'yemek' plus -ten.
The -meli suffix means should or must: 'güvenmelisin' = you should believe in yourself. It attaches straight onto the verb stem.
The -la ending means with: 'arkadaşlarımla' = with my friends. It stacks after the -ım (my) part: 'arkadaş', 'lar', 'ım', 'la'.
The habit ending -r plus -di means used to: 'dinlerdi' = he used to listen. It marks a repeated past habit, not one finished action.
The -den ending marks a source: 'benden' = from me. Learning from someone uses it, so 'öğrenmek' pairs with the -den form.
The -ama inside a verb means cannot: 'alışamadım' = I couldn't get used to it. Without it, 'alışmadım' = I didn't get used to it.
After a number the noun stays singular: 'iki kedi', not 'kediler', and 'bir köpek' stays bare. The number already signals plural.
Negative future is stem plus -ma plus future -acak: 'çıkmayacağız' = we will not go out, from 'çık', 'ma', 'yacağız'.
The verb 'çıkmak' takes the -e form for a goal: 'yürüyüşe çıkarım' = I go out for a walk. The walk carries the -e ending.
The -mış ending marks news you infer or were told, not saw: 'kalmış' = it apparently stayed closed.
